transcript:
Meeting Header:
- Recorded at: 2026-11-14T17:00:00-07:00
- Duration: 62 minutes
- Location: Zoom (recording enabled)
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Oren Patel (Redwood SE), Jared Ortiz (Head of ML - Greenline), Priya Nair (Platform Eng - Greenline), Carlos Mendez (CTO - Greenline)

Summary: quick POC scoping to align on harness integration. Focus on customer's script formats, expected load shape, streaming vs non-streaming call patterns, and success criteria (latency p95, error budget, quality guardrails).

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for taking time. quick roll call?
[00:07] Jared: Jared here
[00:09] Priya: Priya here
[00:11] Carlos: Carlos makes three
[00:13] Maya: great, Oren from our SE team is here too, he'll drive the harness details. um, goal is to leave with a concrete plan to run an initial benchmark with your real scripts.
[00:25] Oren: yeah hi all. real quick on the agenda — 1) understand the script formats and runtime (are these streaming websockets or plain REST calls), 2) size the workload and target SLOs, 3) decide acceptance criteria and run cadence, and 4) surface any security / network blockers.
[00:40] Priya: awesome, we're mostly running a mix. the user facing path is streaming — so clients open a websocket and we stream partial answers back. but we also have server-side batch jobs that call non-streaming endpoints for summarization. so it's mixed-mode.
[00:58] Maya: perfect — that's exactly the kind of complexity Redwood is built for. can you describe your traffic shape? like RPS, typical token lengths, and concurrency?
[01:10] Jared: sure. baseline is about 120 rps during peak, but those are small short chats — like 80 tokens average. we have intermittent spikes to 600 rps during health alerts, and the summarization jobs run in bursts of ~30 concurrent long requests (700-1,200 tokens).
[01:29] Oren: okay so two orthogonal axes — streaming short-chats with high RPS and short tokens, and long-tail batch jobs. for benchmarking we'll want at least two scenario profiles: a streaming steady-state and a mixed-burst profile.
[01:45] Carlos: for acceptance we care about p95 latency under normal peak and p99 under degraded but acceptable conditions. we want p95 < 250ms for chat partials and p95 < 800ms for full non-streaming summary calls. those numbers are kind of hard limits.
[02:03] Maya: noted. and do you have quality thresholds — like hallucination rate tolerance or an eval set?
[02:09] Jared: yes we have a small eval suite, around 120 prompts where we can measure factuality/regression. that's part of our success criteria — we can't sacrifice quality for 10% cost savings.
[02:20] Oren: good. one note on streaming — our runtime provides chunked delta streaming, which has lower perceived latency but more CPU per connection. so when you scale to 600 rps sustained we need to budget for connection concurrency and KV cache size.
[02:36] Priya: when you say KV cache you mean the attention KV cache right? sometimes our infra team calls it K V cash (laughs) because of transcripts in older calls.
[02:45] Oren: yeah that's a classic transcription thing. KV cache = key/value cache for autoregressive decoding. it matters a lot for long-form responses because it reduces repeated compute.
[02:55] Maya: quick security check — you'll need KMS for key wrapping? any SOC 2 or audit constraints?
[03:02] Carlos: SOC 2 is a must. we need audit logs, SSO via SAML, and for the Private deployment option, our security team prefers HSM-backed KMS. but for the initial benchmark we can use hosted with customer-managed keys if that's quicker.
[03:18] Oren: that alignment helps. for the benchmark we usually run in a staging VPC and can either peer with your VPC or run tests from within Redwood Dedicated nodes — depends on which path you prefer. peering will be closer to your production network but takes a couple business days of setup.
[03:35] Priya: peering is fine but we need the checklist. i'll share subnet and egress rules.
[03:40] Maya: great. on the harness side — what format are your scripts in? are they a custom Python harness, k6, or something internal?
[03:47] Jared: we have an internal runner. it's Python-based, wraps websockets and an internal retry/backoff library. scripts are a mixture of line-delimited JSON and protobufs for some telemetry.
[03:59] Oren: okay that's helpful. we can create an adapter — either ingest ndjson or a small shim that replays your websocket events against our endpoint. do you have an example script to share?
[04:10] Jared: yes i'll share two samples: a streaming chat session and a long summary job. note: our streaming messages include interim metadata events every 200ms so the harness must honor that timing.
[04:22] Maya: perfect. that will let Oren build a small adapter. we'll attempt to run the first benchmark using your scripts unmodified, but if there's proprietary protobufs we may ask you to produce a telemetry-to-ndjson export.
[04:35] Priya: we can do that export. one question on metrics — what telemetry do you need? token counts, latency percentiles, CPU/GPU utilization per instance?
[04:45] Oren: all of the above. minimum: request/response latency with p50/p95/p99, tokens per request, error codes, and per-model throughput. optional: GPU util and per-process memory for debugging hot spots.
[04:58] Carlos: and for costs — can you show how batching and quantization recommendations affect unit cost? that's a key decision factor for us.
[05:06] Maya: yes our Optimize toolkit will produce model and quantization suggestions after the benchmark. Oren, we'll capture baseline cost per 1k tokens and simulate different batch windows.
[05:15] Oren: right — for example, at 80-token average chat with continuous batching the per-token compute can drop ~20% but you may see added tail latency in cold-starts. we'll model that in the report.
[05:27] Priya: speaking of cold-starts, our SLA requires <2% of requests hitting cold-start latencies beyond 5s. is that something Redwood can instrument?
[05:36] Oren: yes we can tag cold-starts in traces. we also support warm pool sizing in Dedicated to reduce those events.
[05:43] Maya: let's talk acceptance criteria concretely — I'll read what I heard and you confirm: 1) p95 chat streaming latency < 250ms under normal peak (120 rps), 2) p99 under burst (600 rps) < 2.5s, 3) non-streaming summary p95 < 800ms at 30 concurrent jobs, 4) quality regression on eval set < 2% delta vs baseline, 5) error rate < 0.5% for 24-hour run. is that accurate?
[06:05] Carlos: yes that's accurate, except we want the error rate threshold during a 48-hour run. so extend to 48 hours.
[06:12] Maya: updated to 48 hours. Jared, you earlier mentioned spikes — do you have a predictable schedule for those or are they bursty?
[06:20] Jared: mostly bursty tied to external notifications (health pipeline). they tend to last 10-20 minutes. we'll provide a 48-hour trace that includes a couple spikes.
[06:29] Oren: great. for the harness runbook we'll want a traffic replay, credentials (short-lived), and a guardrail to stop the run if error rates climb >1.5%.
[06:38] Priya: got it. another security question — logs, PII, and retention. our data contains PHI-ish tokens so we need transcript redaction and request-level data masked. does Redwood support masking?
[06:49] Oren: we support token masking and configurable retention windows. for Private deployments we can enforce zero retention. for hosted we can set a 7-day retention with field-level redaction. you'll need to sign the DPA addendum for that.
[07:01] Maya: good note - we'll attach the DPA and SOC2 link in the follow-up email.
[07:06] Carlos: also include any compliance docs for HSM/KMS as pdf links.
[07:10] Maya: will do. back to timeline: what's realistic to run the first benchmark? if we get scripts and traces by 2026-11-20, when can we run?
[07:19] Oren: assuming peering is not blocking, we can ingest artifacts and have an adapter ready by 2026-11-23; run kickoff on 11-23 or 11-24 and run 48-hour benchmark starting 11-25. so results and a report by 11-30.
[07:31] Priya: that timeline works for us if peering completes. if peering slips we might run from dedicated nodes earlier.
[07:38] Jared: question on metrics again — can you produce a per-endpoint cost breakout so we can see per-feature economics?
[07:45] Oren: absolutely, our Console will show token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and per-model. we'll include a CSV export in the benchmark report.
[07:53] Maya: any other blockers?
[07:55] Carlos: one last thing — how do you handle fallback policies? if a model becomes unavailable is there an automated fallback to a smaller variant? we need graceful degradation.
[08:05] Oren: yes, we can route by policy. for POC we'll test a canary fallback — route 5% to a smaller quantized model and measure delta. that's part of the resilience check.
[08:16] Priya: that sounds good. about the harness adapter — how much work is it on our side? do you need protobuf defs?
[08:22] Oren: ideally yes, protobuf defs are easiest. if not, the ndjson export will do. adapter work is typically 1-2 engineer days on our side, and we ask for a point person to validate behavior.
[08:34] Maya: I'll list Oren as owner for adapter and Priya as customer contact.
[08:38] Maya: let me walk through the SLO matrix doc we'll send — columns: scenario, workload (rps/concurrency), token distribution, p50/p95/p99 latencies, error budget, quality metrics, pass/fail. we'll pre-fill with the numbers we discussed and you'll update if needed.
[08:55] Jared: makes sense. do you have a canonical format?
[08:58] Maya: yes it's a simple spreadsheet, we'll share link. I'll also paste a sample harness config snippet in the doc.
[09:04] Priya: about cost modeling — will the report show projected monthly cost at 99th percentile traffic? that's what our finance likes.
[09:12] Oren: we can extrapolate monthly costs using your 24-hr trace normalized to month, include both hosted and dedicated delta.
[09:20] Carlos: and include the effect of quantization choices — int8 vs int4 where available?
[09:25] Oren: we'll include recommended quantization profiles and expected quality delta; however, not all open models have int4 kernels optimized on our runtime — we'll call that out.
[09:33] Maya: quick sanity: do we expect any additional infra changes on your side during benchmark? e.g., firewall rules, rate limits?
[09:40] Priya: firewall will be fine once we peer. we do have an API gateway that imposes a 10k/min burst limit unless we whitelist Redwood IPs — i'll add that to the checklist.
[09:50] Oren: good flag. we'll provide IP ranges.
[09:53] -- [10:15] Middle section: Oren walks through harness adapter example and sample ndjson format (transcribed paraphrase) --
[10:15] Oren: example adapter expects a manifest with fields: session_id, events[], event_type (input|partial|commit), delta_ms. we replay with original timing. in ndjson one line per event.
[10:31] Jared: for streaming partials we already emit interim events with metadata; we want those preserved so client-side UX doesn't regress.
[10:38] Oren: yep we preserve partial sequences. one caveat: if your client expects server-sent event pacing below 50ms we'll need to verify loader performance.
[10:45] Priya: noted.
[10:48] -- [12:02] Short pause while Maya shares SLO spreadsheet link in chat (link: https://redwood.example.com/slo/GLN-draft) --
[12:10] Maya: link is in chat, please check the prefilled numbers.
[12:18] Carlos: opened. looks good.
[12:21] Jared: one more on quality trials — can we pin model versions for the benchmark so we get deterministic comparisons?
[12:28] Oren: yes you can pin a model commit; we'll pin the same variant across runs. for rollback we also capture the model's manifest.
[12:36] Priya: what about tokenization differences across models? we had a mismatch previously when comparing two providers.
[12:42] Oren: we'll normalize using the same tokenizer in the eval harness and report token delta. important for cost comparisons.
[12:49] Maya: do you want us to include a canary A/B test in the 48-hour run? like 90/10 split to measure quality vs cheaper quantized model.
[12:58] Carlos: yes include that as an optional experiment.
[13:02] Maya: okay noted. next, run logistics — we'll need credentials and a short-lived API key with limited scopes. do you prefer to provision keys or have us use a test service account?
[13:12] Priya: we'll provision a test service account and a scoped key for the benchmark.
[13:16] Oren: great. also we ask for a smoke run first — 15 minutes at 50% of target — to validate adapter and metrics pipeline.
[13:25] Jared: makes sense.
[13:27] -- [20:00] Long technical tangent where Oren and Priya discuss backoff logic and idempotency in their internal retry library; transcription includes some mis-heard terms like "replay tokenization" vs "replay topology" --
[20:12] Priya: our backoff uses jitter with a 500ms base; we do idempotent requests by session id.
[20:20] Oren: perfect, that'll map well to our harness which supports jitter and replay windows.
[20:28] -- [30:00] Discussion around tracing and APM integrations; customer requests distributed traces exported to Datadog.
[30:05] Maya: we can ship traces to Datadog — we'll include an example config.
[30:12] Carlos: include a sample trace mapping to our existing spans.
[30:17] Oren: noted.
[30:20] -- [40:00] Pricing and commitment discussion; Maya explains Hosted vs Dedicated delta, burst options, reserved capacity. customer asks for 30-day pilot pricing.
[40:10] Maya: for a 30-day pilot we can offer a discounted reserved bucket for the test, details in the pricing sheet.
[40:18] Carlos: will finance need an estimate for monthly run-rate if we go to production?
[40:22] Maya: yes we'll include an extrapolated estimate in the final report.
[40:27] -- [50:00] Roadblocks recap and confirmation of deliverables.
[50:03] Maya: quick recap: Oren builds adaptor and smoke run w/ provided scripts; customer shares scripts + 48-hr trace + peering checklist; Redwood shares SLO spreadsheet + pricing + DPA and SOC2 docs; schedule benchmark kickoff 11-23.
[50:20] Jared: correct.
[50:22] Priya: will get the artifacts uploaded by 11-20.
[50:26] Maya: any last questions?
[50:28] Carlos: none from me. thanks.
[50:31] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the doc links and action items.
[61:30] (meeting ends)

References shared in chat:
- SLO spreadsheet: https://redwood.example.com/slo/GLN-draft
- Draft harness adapter example: https://redwood.example.com/harness/adapters/gln-shim
- SOC2 & DPA: https://redwood.example.com/compliance/soc2.pdf

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-hears (K V cash for KV cache), speaker overlap at 00:25 and 10:31, some technical terms abbreviated or spelled out (SAML as sam-el in early portion).

End of transcript.
